title: Two Hours of Strength Training a Week May Be the Sweet Spot for Living Longer — and the Evidence Is Now Hard to Ignore
excerpt: A pair of landmark Harvard studies spanning 150,000 adults and 30 years found that 90–120 minutes of weekly resistance exercise reduced mortality by up to 13 percent — and combining it with cardio cut the risk nearly in half.
body:
For decades, public health advice on exercise has leaned heavily on aerobic activity — brisk walking, running, cycling, swimming. Strength training was treated as a nice-to-have, something for athletes and gym enthusiasts, not a longevity essential.

Two new studies from Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health, published within weeks of each other, suggest that view is badly outdated. The data now points to a surprisingly modest weekly strength-training target that may meaningfully extend your life.

## The Sweet Spot: 90 to 120 Minutes

The first study, published in the *British Journal of Sports Medicine*, tracked more than 147,000 adults across three long-running cohorts — the Health Professionals Follow-Up Study, the Nurses' Health Study, and the Nurses' Health Study II — for up to 30 years.

Adults who averaged 90 to 120 minutes of weekly resistance training — activities such as pushups, squats, lunges, or weightlifting — had a **13 percent lower risk of death from any cause** compared with those who did none. The reduction was even steeper for specific causes: a **19 percent lower risk of cardiovascular death** and a **27 percent lower risk of neurological diseases** like Alzheimer's.

Critically, doing more than two hours a week did not produce additional benefits. The curve flattened beyond 120 minutes, meaning longer gym sessions may build more muscle but don't appear to buy more years.

"Importantly, 90 to 120 minutes per week should not be interpreted as a strict target or threshold," cautioned lead author Yiwen Zhang, a postdoctoral fellow at Harvard Chan. "But the takeaway is that you don't need to live in the gym."

## Women See an Even Sharper Heart Benefit

A second, related study — published in *JACC*, the flagship journal of the American College of Cardiology — analysed 117,000 women from the same Nurses' Health cohorts and found that women who did two or more hours of weekly strength training had a **20 percent lower risk of cardiovascular disease** and a **14 percent lower risk of heart attack** per additional hour.

When those women also met the standard aerobic guideline of 150 minutes per week, the combined benefit was dramatic: a **45 percent lower risk of heart attack** compared with inactive women.

"Resistance training is thought to improve cholesterol, insulin sensitivity, and overall body composition — all of which are strongly linked to coronary artery disease," the study's co-authors, Tianyue Zhang and Edward Giovannucci, said.

This matters particularly for women during and after menopause, when muscle loss and cardiovascular risk accelerate simultaneously. Board-certified cardiologist Mary Greene of Manhattan Cardiology noted that resistance training "addresses multiple morbidities simultaneously — osteoporosis, frailty, fall risk, and heart disease."

## You Don't Need a Gym

Both studies make an encouraging practical point: even small amounts of strength training provided measurable benefits. Participants who did as little as 30 minutes a week showed lower cancer-related mortality.

The activities counted as strength training were broad — body-weight exercises at home, resistance bands, free weights, or machines. No gym membership required.

Clarinda Hougen, a sports medicine specialist at Cedars-Sinai, recommended starting with "simple body weight exercises like squats, step-ups, modified pushups, and planks. Aim for two to three sessions per week and focus on proper form. As you build strength, you can add resistance with dumbbells, kettlebells, or bands."

## Why This Matters for the South Asian Diaspora

For NRIs and the broader South Asian diaspora, these findings land with particular urgency. South Asians carry disproportionately high rates of cardiovascular disease, Type 2 diabetes, and metabolic syndrome — all conditions where muscle mass and metabolic health play protective roles. A 2023 *Lancet* analysis found that South Asians develop heart disease roughly a decade earlier than Western populations.

Yet strength training remains culturally underemphasised in many South Asian communities, where walking is the default exercise and lifting weights is sometimes seen as unnecessary or even risky for older adults. These studies suggest the opposite: resistance exercise may be among the highest-return health investments available, especially for populations with elevated metabolic risk.

The prescription is modest — two to three sessions a week, 15 to 20 minutes each — and the evidence backing it now spans three decades and more than 150,000 people. For diaspora families managing ageing parents' health remotely, encouraging a simple home strength routine may be one of the most practical interventions available.

## What's Next

The researchers acknowledged limitations: exercise was self-reported, and the studies couldn't capture workout intensity or structure. Future studies will aim to refine the optimal dose, type, and intensity of resistance training across different populations.

But the direction is clear. As cardiologist Rigved Tadwalkar of Pacific Heart Institute put it: "I would not tell a patient that lifting weights guarantees a 20 percent reduction in risk. But I would tell her that strength training now has a stronger cardiovascular case than many people realise."

*Sources: British Journal of Sports Medicine (June 2026); JACC (June 2026); Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health; Healthline*
